sections.figure_alt: The z-plane with poles inside the unit circle.
sections.body_md:
Discrete-time systems operate on sampled data: the state updates at fixed intervals \(T\) seconds apart. Instead of differential equations, we have difference equations. Instead of the s-plane, we use the z-plane.

Stability shifts from the left half-plane to the inside of the unit circle. A pole at \(z = 0.9\) is stable (decaying); a pole at \(z = 1.1\) is unstable (growing). The mapping \(z = e^{sT}\) connects continuous and discrete poles. Faster sampling (smaller \(T\)) moves poles closer to \(z = 1\).

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Difference equation: \(x[k+1] = A_d x[k] + B_d u[k]\).

Discretization of \(s\)-plane pole: \(z = e^{sT}\).

A pole at \(s = -a\) maps to \(z = e^{-aT}\).

Stability: all poles inside \(|z| < 1\).

Nyquist frequency: \(f_N = 1/(2T)\). Frequencies above \(f_N\) alias.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A continuous system has pole at \(s = -4\) with sample time \(T = 0.1\) s. The discrete pole is \(z = e^{-4 \times 0.1} = e^{-0.4} = 0.67\). This is inside the unit circle, so the discrete mode decays. The decay per sample is 0.67, meaning each step the mode loses about 33% of its value. After 10 samples (1 s), the mode is at \(0.67^{10} = 0.018\), consistent with \(e^{-4 \times 1} = 0.018\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Aliasing occurs when sampling below the Nyquist rate. Frequencies above \(f_N = 1/(2T)\) fold back and appear as low-frequency artifacts. Numerical issues arise when \(T\) is very small compared to the system time constants, as poles cluster near \(z = 1\). Computational delay of one sample is \(z^{-1}\), which adds phase lag.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Digital PID requires discretization (Tustin, forward Euler, backward Euler). Z-transform analysis mirrors Laplace methods. Multirate systems sample different signals at different rates. Anti-aliasing filters are essential before sampling. The bilinear (Tustin) transform preserves frequency-domain characteristics.
